# Oceans claim verification checklist

> Generated by `npm run verify:report` from `content/`. Do not edit by hand; record results with the commands below and regenerate.

**Progress:** 0 / 598 claims fully verified · 0 verified, 776 unverified, 0 incorrect, 0 unsupported (776 claim–source checks).

## How to verify

1. Open the source URL. Each section below is one source page with every claim that cites it.
2. For each claim, find the sentence on the page that supports it. Numbers must match (rounding like "about" is fine; a different figure is not).
3. Record the result (or fill in the CSV and run `npm run verify:import-csv -- docs/verification/oceans.csv --by "Your Name"`):
   - **verified**: the page states it. Paste the supporting sentence as the quote.
   - **unsupported**: the page does not say it. Find a better source or change the claim.
   - **incorrect**: the page (or better evidence) contradicts it. The card/question must be revised in a new revision.
4. A level can only be published when every claim it states or teaches is verified against every source it cites. `npm run validate:content` enforces this.

"Pre-check" notes were written while drafting. They point at what to look at closely. They are not verification.

"Fact-check" results come from an automated check against independent sources found by web search (not the cited page, which couldn't be opened). A **corrected** or **disputed** claim was reworded to match those sources; the old wording is shown. They are not verification either: the cited page still has to be checked.

- **Source:** `source.aad_crabeater_seal`
- **URL:** https://www.antarctica.gov.au/about-antarctica/animals/seals/crabeater-seal/

### ☐ `fact.oceans.crabeater_krill_teeth`: unverified

> **Claim:** Crabeater seals eat krill, not crabs: their specially adapted teeth have extra projections that strain krill from gulped seawater.

- **Concept:** Sea ice as a seal's home (`concept.oceans.iceseal_ice_home`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L77 “Seals on the Ice” · `card.oceans.077.c4` (fact): Crabeater seals don't eat crabs. They eat krill. / Their teeth have extra projections that work like a sieve: gulp seawater, strain out Level 75's krill. They spend their whole lives on the pack ice around Antarctica, resting and breeding on it, and they're the most abundant seal in the Southern Ocean. Whoever named them wasn't watching lunch.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Polar Seas” · `card.oceans.080.c2` (comparison): Two polar seas, side by side: The Arctic (A fresh top layer helps sea ice grow; Year-round whales: beluga, narwhal, bowhead; Polar bears hunt ringed seals on the ice) vs The Southern Ocean (A current flows west to east around Antarctica; Fish with antifreeze proteins; Krill feed penguins, whales and fish; Crabeaters strain krill; Weddell seals chew holes)
- **Tested by:**
  - L77 `question.oceans.077.q3`: Level 75 said krill feed many polar animals. How is a crabeater seal built to eat them? → **Teeth with extra projections that sieve krill**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The Antarctic and Southern Ocean Coalition's crabeater page and Oceanwide Expeditions both describe lobed, sieve-like teeth that filter krill, which makes up most of the diet. Sources: https://www.asoc.org/learn/crabeater-seal/, https://oceanwide-expeditions.com/blog/the-crabeater-seals-of-antarctica

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.oceans.crabeater_krill_teeth source.aad_crabeater_seal --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

### ☐ `fact.oceans.krill_under_ice_winter`: unverified

> **Claim:** Young krill overwinter under the sea ice, where the complex underside of the ice gives them shelter from predators and access to food; winter sea ice is their nursery and feeding habitat.

- **Concept:** Sea ice: the krill nursery (`concept.oceans.krill_sea_ice_nursery`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L75 “Krill” · `card.oceans.075.c4` (text): A nursery under the ice / Winter is the hard part. Young krill spend it under the sea ice, where the rough, complex underside of the ice gives them shelter from predators and access to food. Scientists call winter sea ice the krill's nursery and feeding ground. Remember Level 72's ice that grows every winter? For a young krill, that's the roof over its head.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Polar Seas” · `card.oceans.080.c4` (text): Ice from sea, ice from land / Put it together. Sea ice freezes from seawater and squeezes out its salt; icebergs are frozen fresh water from glaciers, built from snow. Ice is only about 9% less dense than water, which is why both float and a berg hides most of itself. And under the southern sea ice, young krill spend the winter. The ice isn't just scenery; it's the floor, the roof and the nursery of the polar seas.
- **Tested by:**
  - L75 `question.oceans.075.q3`: From Level 72, sea ice grows every winter. Why does that winter ice matter to young krill? → **They shelter and feed under it**
  - L80 `question.oceans.080.q5`: Polar Seas recap, from Levels 75 and 79: why could losing winter sea ice matter to the whole Southern Ocean food web? → **Young krill, the main food of many animals, winter under it**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NSIDC's 'Why sea ice matters' says sea ice is a platform for algae that fuel the food web; the ScienceDirect krill winter-diet literature notes krill feed on ice algae in winter. Sources: https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/sea-ice/why-sea-ice-matters, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2023.1107567/full

### ☐ `fact.oceans.argo_thousands`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Argo program deploys thousands of floats across the world's ocean; its 3,000-float goal was reached in November 2007.

- **Concept:** Argo floats (`concept.oceans.satellite_argo_floats`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L89 “Satellites Watch the Sea” · `card.oceans.089.c4` (text): Robots below the surface / Satellites only see the sea's skin, so the Argo program sends down thousands of robot floats. Each drifts about 1 km deep. Every ten days it sinks to 2 km, then rises, measuring temperature and salinity, and radios its data to a satellite. It changes depth by pumping oil in and out of an outside bladder: Level 87's ballast trick. Argo is named for Jason's ship, because the floats work with the Jason satellites.
- **Tested by:**
  - L89 `question.oceans.089.q2`: Satellites already watch the whole ocean. Why does the Argo program still need floats? → **Satellites only see the surface; floats measure down to 2 km**
  - L89 `question.oceans.089.q3`: An Argo float sinks and rises by pumping oil in and out of an outside bladder. Which Level 87 idea is it using? → **Changing buoyancy, like ballast tanks**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The Argo FAQ and WMO say the array has about 4,000 floats worldwide. Sources: https://argo.ucsd.edu/faq/, https://wmo.int/media/news/argo-ocean-floats-achieve-2-million-profiles-20-years-support-new-research-ocean-heat

> **Claim:** Waves generally become breakers where the water depth is about 1.3 times the wave height.

- **Concept:** Why waves break (`concept.oceans.wave_breaking`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L22 “Why Waves Break” · `card.oceans.022.c3` (text): The top outruns the bottom / Friction holds back the bottom of the wave, but the crest keeps its speed. The front grows steeper and steeper until the crest is racing ahead with no water underneath it, and it topples forward. That's a breaker. As a rule of thumb, it happens where the water is about 1.3 times as deep as the wave is tall: a 1 m wave breaks in water about 1.3 m deep.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Waves and Tides” · `card.oceans.030.c3` (comparison): Three ways the sea rises: Wind waves (Wind speed, time and fetch set their size; Swell: crests more than 10 to 12 seconds apart; Break where the water is about 1.3 times their height deep) vs Tides (Moon and Sun; the Sun's pull a little under half; A crest a little over every 12 hours; Up to 16 m in the Bay of Fundy) vs Storm surge (A storm's winds push water ashore; Surge plus tide makes the storm tide)

  - L22 `question.oceans.022.q3`: From Level 21: swell can cross an ocean with little energy lost. Where does that long trip finally end? → **In shallow water, where the slowed wave breaks**
  - L30 `question.oceans.030.q4`: Waves and tides recap, from Level 22: a 2 m wave heads for shore. About how deep is the water where it breaks? → **About 2.6 m**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. University of Hawaii Exploring Our Fluid Earth gives the equivalent criterion: a wave breaks when its height exceeds three-fourths of the water depth (depth about 1.33 times height). ### ☐ `fact.oceans.spreading_hess_1960`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1960, geophysicist Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading: new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and old ocean floor sinks back into the trenches, so the ocean basins are constantly recycled and Earth doesn't get bigger.

- **Concept:** The sea floor's conveyor belt (`concept.oceans.seafloor_spreading_cycle`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c2` (text): A conveyor belt of rock / In 1960, geophysicist Harry Hess proposed an answer: seafloor spreading. New ocean floor forms at the mid-ocean ridges, where Level 13's magma rises. Old ocean floor sinks back down into the trenches of Level 14. The ocean basins are constantly recycled, which is also why Earth doesn't keep getting bigger. Ridges are where the conveyor belt comes out; trenches are where it goes back in.
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c3` (text): Stripes on the sea floor / The evidence was written in magnetism. As lava cools into rock, grains of a magnetic mineral called magnetite lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field, and that field has flipped many times. So the ocean floor carries stripes of alternating magnetic direction, running parallel to the ridge and matching on both sides of it. New rock forms in the middle and moves off both ways, like a barcode printed twice in mirror image.
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c4` (text): Older, deeper, gone / Walk away from a ridge and the floor gets older: youngest at the crest, older farther out. Level 15's guyots showed it sinks as it travels, too. Very little ocean floor is older than 150 million years, and the oldest known, about 200 million years old, lies in the far western Pacific. After that, it's back down a trench.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: The Ocean Floor” · `card.oceans.020.c4` (text): Minus 6,000 m: only the trenches / By 6,000 m, most of the ocean is gone. The flat abyssal plains lie bare under their blanket of ooze, and only the trenches still hold water, down to about 11 km at Challenger Deep. That's where old sea floor sinks back down, while the ridges make new floor. Drained, the floor tells one story: made at the ridges, buried in snow, swallowed by the trenches.
- **Tested by:**
  - L18 `question.oceans.018.q1`: In seafloor spreading, what happens to old ocean floor? → **It sinks back down into the trenches**
  - L18 `question.oceans.018.q3`: From Level 15: guyots are old islands now 1,000 to 2,000 m down. What does seafloor spreading add to their story? → **The floor sinks as it moves from the ridge, carrying them down**
  - L20 `question.oceans.020.q3`: Ocean Floor recap, from Level 18: why is no ocean floor older than about 200 million years? → **Old floor sinks back into trenches as ridges make new floor**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. USGS This Dynamic Earth describes Hess's early-1960s idea that crust made at ridges is consumed in trenches, explaining why Earth does not grow; NOAA Science On a Sphere describes the same recycling. Sources: https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/developing.html, https://sos.noaa.gov/catalog/datasets/age-of-the-seafloor/

### ☐ `fact.oceans.sky_reflection_surface`: unverified

> **Claim:** The sea's surface does reflect the sky, which is why big bodies of water look gray on overcast days, but the color of the sea and of the sky arise separately.

- **Concept:** Why the ocean is blue (`concept.oceans.ocean_blue_absorption`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L7 “Why the Ocean Is Blue” · `card.oceans.007.c3` (text): But isn't it just the sky? / Partly, right at the surface. The sea does reflect the sky, which is why a big stretch of water looks gray on an overcast day. But the color of the sea and the color of the sky arise separately. The deep blue comes from water absorbing red light, the same reason a glass of it looks clear while a whole sea looks blue.
- **Tested by:**
  - L7 `question.oceans.007.q2`: Why does a glass of seawater look clear when the sea it came from looks blue? → **Water's own blue is too faint in small amounts**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Scientific American: the color of the ocean and the color of the sky are related but occur independently of each other. Sources: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-does-the-ocean-appear/, https://www.whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-facts/why-is-the-ocean-blue/

> **Claim:** The ocean has taken up about 91% of the extra heat trapped in the climate system; the atmosphere got about 1% (IPCC, 2021).

- **Appears in:**
  - L36 “The Ocean's Heat” · `card.oceans.036.c3` (fact): The ocean has taken up about 91% of the extra heat trapped in the climate system. / That's the IPCC's 2021 figure, and the atmosphere, where we live, got only about 1%. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.salt_evaporation_leaves_salt`: unverified

> **Claim:** When ocean water evaporates the salts are left behind, so salt builds up in the sea; river water carries dissolved salt too, but far too little to taste.

- **Concept:** Where sea salt comes from (`concept.oceans.salt_sources`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L5 “Why the Sea Is Salty” · `card.oceans.005.c3` (text): Rivers deliver, the sea keeps / Rain holds a little dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic, so over time it breaks down rocks on land. Streams and rivers carry the freed salts to the sea. River water has salt in it too, just far too little to taste. At sea, water evaporates but the salt is left behind, so delivery after delivery, it builds up. The river passes the salt along; the ocean hangs on to it.
- **Tested by:**
  - L5 `question.oceans.005.q2`: Rivers bring salt to the sea, yet river water tastes fresh. Why does the sea end up salty? → **Evaporation removes water but leaves the salt**
  - L5 `question.oceans.005.q3`: From Level 1: water rising off the ocean falls again as rain, including over land. What does that rain do before it flows back to the sea? → **Breaks down rocks and carries their salts along**
  - L61 `question.oceans.061.q3`: From Level 5: rain breaks down rock and rivers carry the salt to the sea. What else do those same rivers carry to the coast? → **Worn-down bits of rock that become sand**
  - L67 `question.oceans.067.q3`: From Level 5: rivers carry salts freed from rock into the sea. Where do mollusks get the building blocks for their shells? → **From calcium and carbonate in seawater**
  - L95 `question.oceans.095.q3`: From Level 5: rain and rivers carry salts from rocks to the sea. What else does runoff carry there, according to this level? → **Pollution such as engine oil and fertilizer**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. USGS: ions not used by organisms are left over and their concentrations increase over time, which is how the delivered salt builds up in the sea. Sources: https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/why-ocean-salty

### ☐ `fact.oceans.seawater_weighs_more`: unverified

> **Claim:** At 10°C, a liter of fresh water weighs 1,000 g and a liter of seawater about 1,026 g, about 26 g more.

- **Concept:** Seawater stacks by density (`concept.oceans.density_layers`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L6 “Layers of Water” · `card.oceans.006.c1` (text): A liter of seawater weighs about 26 g more than a liter of fresh water. / That small difference is enough to sort the whole ocean into layers, like a drink that refuses to mix.
  - L6 “Layers of Water” · `card.oceans.006.c2` (text): Two ways to get heavier / Water gets denser in two ways. Cool it down: cold water is denser than warm water. Add salt: salty water is denser than fresh water. At 10°C, a liter of fresh water weighs 1,000 g and a liter of seawater about 1,026 g. So the heaviest water in the sea is the cold, salty kind, and the lightest is warm and fresh.
- **Tested by:**
  - L6 `question.oceans.006.q3`: From Level 5: dissolved salts make up about 3.5% of seawater's weight. What does that salt do to seawater's density? → **Raises it: seawater is denser than fresh water**
  - L33 `question.oceans.033.q3`: Level 6 showed that salty water is denser than fresh. Why could extra fresh water from rain and melting ice slow the AMOC? → **Fresher surface water is lighter, so less of it sinks**
  - L72 `question.oceans.072.q3`: From Level 6: the salty water pushed out by growing sea ice is also very cold. What does it do? → **It sinks, because it is denser**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. WHOI gives fresh water at 1 g/cc and seawater at 1.02 to 1.03 g/cc, consistent with 1,026 g per liter. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.foam_cup_shrinks`: unverified

> **Claim:** Oceanographers send decorated foam cups into the deep; pressure squeezes the tiny air pockets in the foam, and the cups come back shrunken for good.

- **Concept:** Pressure crushes air spaces (`concept.oceans.pressure_squeezes_air`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L9 “Pressure” · `card.oceans.009.c1` (text): Send a foam cup to the deep sea and it comes back doll-sized. / Oceanographers decorate foam cups and send them down with their deep-sea gear. The cups come back shrunken, and they stay that way. Nothing touched them but water. So what squeezed them?
  - L9 “Pressure” · `card.oceans.009.c4` (text): Why the cup shrinks / Water itself barely squeezes, but air does. Foam is full of tiny air pockets, and deep-sea pressure crushes them, so the cup shrinks and never bounces back. Your lungs and the air spaces in your head are air pockets too, and enough pressure would collapse them. That shrunken cup is a warning in miniature.
  - L88 “The Deepest Dive” · `card.oceans.088.c2` (text): A balloon in the sea / Trieste hung from a huge float filled with gasoline. Gasoline is lighter than water, so it gave lift, and it barely compresses, so the deep couldn't crush the float the way it shrank Level 9's foam cup. ## Why are there so many giants in the deep sea? (Live Science)

### ☐ `fact.oceans.deep_gigantism_cold_slow`: unverified

> **Claim:** Cold deep water slows animals' metabolisms, and many deep-sea creatures grow and mature very slowly, which may help them reach large sizes.

- **Concept:** Deep-sea gigantism (`concept.oceans.deep_gigantism`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L58 “Deep-Sea Giants” · `card.oceans.058.c3` (text): Slow and steady / Scientists aren't sure what drives it, and several causes may work together. One is the cold: chilly deep water slows animals' metabolisms, and many deep-sea creatures grow and mature very slowly. Another is that few predators bother a big, armored isopod, so it can take its time. Growing up slowly, it turns out, can mean growing up big.
  - L60 “Checkpoint: The Deep” · `card.oceans.060.c4` (text): Cold and hunger: go slow, think big / The midnight zone holds a steady 4°C, and cold slows bodies down. Hunters like the anglerfish wait with a lure instead of chasing, many animals grow large to go farther between meals, and some neighborhoods skip sunlight entirely, living on whale bones and vent chemicals. The deep rewards patience.
- **Tested by:**
  - L58 `question.oceans.058.q3`: Level 51's midnight zone stays at a steady 4°C. How might that cold help deep-sea animals grow large? → **Cold slows metabolism, so they grow slowly**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia's deep-sea gigantism and Bathynomus articles link cold water to larger cells, longer lifespans and larger size. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep-sea_gigantism, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathynomus_giganteus

> **Claim:** The most common cause of lung injury in scuba diving is holding the breath while rising, so divers must breathe out freely during ascent.

### ☐ `fact.oceans.scuba_bends_prevention`: unverified

> **Claim:** Divers prevent the bends by limiting depth, dive time and ascent speed, and many make a safety stop of a few minutes at about 4.5 m below the surface.

- **Appears in:**
  - L86 “Scuba” · `card.oceans.086.c4` (text): The bends / Pressure has a slower trick. Each breath at depth packs in more gas, and the extra nitrogen builds up in your blood and tissues. Rise too fast and it forms bubbles, like a shaken soda opened too quickly: decompression sickness, or the bends. Divers avoid it by limiting depth and time, rising slowly, and often pausing a few minutes about 4.5 m below the surface.

Harvard Health advises rising slowly and not staying deep too long; Dive Training Magazine says safety stops are usually made at 15-20 feet for three to five minutes. Sources: https://www.health.harvard.edu/a_to_z/decompression-sickness-a-to-z, https://dtmag.com/thelibrary/a-safe-habit-safety-stops-as-standard-procedure/

### ☐ `fact.oceans.tides_spring_alignment`: unverified

> **Claim:** Twice a month, at new and full moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine, making higher high tides and lower low tides: spring tides.

- **Appears in:**

Their pulls add together: higher high tides and lower low tides. These are spring tides, named for the tide springing forth, not for the season. About seven days later, at the quarter moons, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and partly cancel. Those are neap tides: the highs a little lower, the lows a little higher. / Lined up: spring tides. Right angles: neap tides.
  - L29 “Storm Surges” · `card.oceans.029.c3` (text): Surge plus tide / The surge doesn't replace the tide; it rides on top of it. Forecasters call the total the storm tide: surge plus the normal astronomical tide. So timing matters. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.intertidal_high_middle`: unverified

> **Claim:** The high tide zone is underwater only at high tide, so it is hotter and drier; the middle zone is covered and uncovered for about equal amounts of time.

- **Appears in:**
  - L27 “Life Between the Tides” · `card.oceans.027.c2` (text): A home that floods on schedule / The intertidal zone is the strip where the ocean meets the land, between high and low tide. Its middle floods and drains twice a day. Living here means surviving swings in moisture, temperature and saltiness, and taking a pounding from waves. The higher up the rock you live, the longer you spend in the air: the high zone is underwater only at high tide, so it's hotter and drier. Imagine a house that floods twice a day, then bakes in between.
  - L27 “Life Between the Tides” · `card.oceans.027.c3` (text): Four floors of the shore / From the top down: the spray zone is only splashed, except in extreme high tides and storms. The high zone, underwater only at high tide, is home to hardy barnacles, snails and limpets. The middle zone spends about equal time wet and dry; mussels, sea stars and anemones live here. The low zone is almost always underwater, uncovered only by the lowest spring tides, and it holds the greatest variety of life, because it suits creatures that can't take long in the air.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA: the high intertidal zone is flooded during high tides but dry between them; the middle zone goes through the tide cycle twice a day. Sources: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/intertidal-zone.html

### ☐ `fact.oceans.trench_subduction`: unverified

> **Claim:** Ocean trenches form by subduction: where plates converge, the older, denser plate is pushed down beneath the lighter one and plunges into the mantle.

- **Concept:** Ocean trenches (`concept.oceans.ocean_trenches`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L14 “Trenches” · `card.oceans.014.c2` (text): Where the sea floor goes back down / Trenches form where two plates converge. The older, denser plate is pushed down beneath the lighter one and plunges into the mantle, and the sea floor above the bend becomes a long, narrow, very deep trench. Most trenches are in the Pacific. If Level 13's ridges are where plates push apart to build sea floor, trenches are where sea floor heads back down into Earth.
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c2` (text): A conveyor belt of rock / In 1960, geophysicist Harry Hess proposed an answer: seafloor spreading. New ocean floor forms at the mid-ocean ridges, where Level 13's magma rises. Old ocean floor sinks back down into the trenches of Level 14. The ocean basins are constantly recycled, which is also why Earth doesn't keep getting bigger. Ridges are where the conveyor belt comes out; trenches are where it goes back in.
- **Tested by:**
  - L14 `question.oceans.014.q1`: How do deep ocean trenches form? → **One plate is pushed down beneath another**

Remember Level 9: pressure comes from the water above you, about one atmosphere per 10 m. Pacific water and rivers in Russia and Canada give it a cold, fresher top layer. Remember Level 6: less salty water is less dense, so it floats on top. That light, fresh lid helps more sea ice grow in the Arctic than around Antarctica.

- **URL:** https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/biggestocean.html
- **License:** US_gov_public_domain · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.oceans.ocean_size_ranking`: unverified

> **Claim:** After the Pacific, the ocean basins rank by size as the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and, smallest, the Arctic.

- **Concept:** The five named oceans by size (`concept.oceans.five_oceans_ranked`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Five Oceans” · `card.oceans.003.c2` (comparison): Five oceans, biggest first: The giant (Pacific: by far the largest; Holds more than half of Earth's free water; All the continents could fit inside it) vs The middle three (Atlantic: second largest; Indian: third; Southern: fourth, circling Antarctica) vs The little one (Arctic: the smallest of all)
- **Tested by:**
  - L3 `question.oceans.003.q1`: Which of the five named oceans is the smallest? → **The Arctic**
  - L3 `question.oceans.003.q3`: From Level 1: if the Pacific holds more than half of Earth's free water, why isn't it a separate ocean from the Atlantic? → **They connect; the border is a line people drew**
  - L21 `question.oceans.021.q3`: From Level 3: all the continents could fit into the Pacific. What did Munk's team find when swell crossed it from New Zealand to Alaska? → **The waves lost very little energy on the way**
  - L81 `question.oceans.081.q3`: From Level 3, the Pacific is by far the largest ocean. By when had voyagers settled its far corners, Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa? → **By about 1300 CE**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. WorldAtlas ranks the oceans by area in the same order: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic (about 15.6 million square km, the smallest). Sources: https://www.worldatlas.com/oceans/the-oceans-of-the-world-by-size-55849.html, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borders_of_the_oceans

### ☐ `fact.oceans.krill_blue_whale_diet`: unverified

> **Claim:** The blue whale, the largest animal known to have lived, feeds almost only on krill and may eat up to 6 tons of it a day.

- **Concept:** Krill: the Southern Ocean's link (`concept.oceans.krill_keystone`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L75 “Krill” · `card.oceans.075.c3` (text): Everybody's lunch / Krill graze on microscopic algae, and they are the main food for many of the Southern Ocean's bigger animals: penguins, whales and fish. That makes them the link between the smallest living things and the biggest. The blue whale, the largest animal known to have lived, eats almost nothing but krill, up to 6 tons of them a day. The giant runs on the tiny.
- **Tested by:**
  - L75 `question.oceans.075.q2`: Why do so many of the Southern Ocean's larger animals depend on krill? → **Krill are their main food, linking them to tiny algae**
  - L76 `question.oceans.076.q3`: A humpback strains its polar summer meal through its baleen. Which Level 75 animal is a main item on that menu? → **Krill**
  - L77 `question.oceans.077.q3`: Level 75 said krill feed many polar animals. How is a crabeater seal built to eat them? → **Teeth with extra projections that sieve krill**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The Smithsonian Ocean portal and WWF both describe blue whales eating up to about 4 tonnes (some say 6 US tons) of krill a day as the largest animal ever known. Sources: https://ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/marine-mammals/blue-whale, https://www.worldwildlife.org/species/blue-whale

### ☐ `fact.oceans.sunlit_dolphin_echolocation`: unverified

> **Claim:** Dolphins use echolocation to fill in what they cannot see: they send out sounds and read the echoes, focusing them with the melon on their forehead, and can interpret signals from half a mile (about 800 m) away.

- **Concept:** Dolphins hunt with sound (`concept.oceans.sunlit_dolphin_echolocation`)

They send out sounds, focus them with the melon (that big rounded forehead) and read the echoes that bounce back. NOAA says a dolphin can interpret echolocation signals from about half a mile (roughly 800 m) away. It's a flashlight made of sound, and it works in the dark. / Send a sound · catch the echo · picture the fish
- **Tested by:**
  - L46 `question.oceans.046.q2`: Why does hunting by echolocation suit dolphins so well in the sea? → **Sound travels fast and far in seawater, even where light fails**

## What is the global ocean conveyor belt? (NOAA National Ocean Service)

- **Source:** `source.noaa_conveyor_belt`
- **URL:** https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/conveyor.html
- **License:** US_gov_public_domain · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.oceans.conveyor_sinks_north`: unverified

> **Claim:** In the far North Atlantic, water chilled by Arctic air grows cold, salty and dense and sinks; surface water moves in to replace it, creating a current.

- **Concept:** The global ocean conveyor (`concept.oceans.conveyor_thermohaline`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L33 “The Great Ocean Conveyor” · `card.oceans.033.c2` (text): Where the ocean sinks / In the far North Atlantic, the water is chilled by Arctic air. When sea ice forms, the salt doesn't freeze; it's left behind in the water around the ice. Now that water is cold and extra salty, so it's dense, and it sinks toward the bottom. Surface water moves in to replace it, and that creates a current. Freezing a bit of sea helps power a planet-sized pump.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Currents and Climate” · `card.oceans.040.c3` (text): The trip / Winds push our parcel along the surface into the Gulf Stream, which carries it north along Florida and then northeast across the Atlantic. In the cold far north it hands its heat to the air, and westerly winds carry that warmth to Europe. Now cold and salty, it sinks and joins the deep conveyor, where one lap takes about 1,000 years.
- **Tested by:**
  - L33 `question.oceans.033.q2`: Why does sea ice forming in the far North Atlantic help drive the ocean conveyor? → **Its salt stays behind, so the water gets denser**
  - L40 `question.oceans.040.q2`: Currents and Climate recap: in what order does our warm parcel travel? → **Wind-driven current, Gulf Stream north, then sinking into the conveyor**
  - L40 `question.oceans.040.q3`: Currents and Climate recap, from Level 33: what makes water sink in the far North Atlantic? → **It's cold and extra salty, so it's dense**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The Met Office describes the AMOC's warm water flowing north, cooling, becoming denser and sinking deep, then spreading south; NOAA's conveyor page gives the Norwegian Sea as the start. Sources: https://weather.metoffice.gov.uk/learn-about/weather/oceans/amoc, https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/conveyor.html

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.oceans.conveyor_sinks_north source.noaa_conveyor_belt --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

### ☐ `fact.oceans.gulf_stream_heat_north`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Gulf Stream is the Atlantic's main conveyor of heat from south to north; in the cold far north its warm water heats the air above it.

In the cold far north, its warm water heats the air above it, and prevailing westerly winds carry that warmth and moisture onto northwestern Europe. The result: Bergen, Norway, gets milder winters than New York, which lies much further south. Same ocean, opposite side of the radiator.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Currents and Climate” · `card.oceans.040.c3` (text): The trip / Winds push our parcel along the surface into the Gulf Stream, which carries it north along Florida and then northeast across the Atlantic. In the cold far north it hands its heat to the air, and westerly winds carry that warmth to Europe. Now cold and salty, it sinks and joins the deep conveyor, where one lap takes about 1,000 years.

Britannica says the Gulf Stream's continuation carries warm water toward northwestern Europe; NOAA's conveyor page says Gulf Stream water heats the atmosphere in the cold northern latitudes. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/place/Gulf-Stream, https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/conveyor.html

### ☐ `fact.oceans.conveyor_1000_years`: unverified

> **Claim:** The global conveyor belt moves at a few centimeters per second, and any given cubic meter of water takes about 1,000 years to complete the journey.

- **Concept:** The global ocean conveyor (`concept.oceans.conveyor_thermohaline`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L33 “The Great Ocean Conveyor” · `card.oceans.033.c1` (text): One cubic meter of seawater takes about 1,000 years to lap the ocean. / No wind pushes it. The engine is something you met in Level 6: cold, salty water is heavy, and heavy water sinks.
  - L33 “The Great Ocean Conveyor” · `card.oceans.033.c3` (text): The slowest current on Earth / This deep, slow circulation is called thermohaline circulation: thermo for temperature, haline for salt, because density differences from both drive it. The global conveyor belt it forms moves at a few centimeters per second. At that crawl, any given cubic meter of water takes about 1,000 years to complete the journey. Water sinking this year won't finish the loop for about ten centuries. / Driven by heat and salt · about 1,000 years per lap
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Currents and Climate” · `card.oceans.040.c3` (text): The trip / Winds push our parcel along the surface into the Gulf Stream, which carries it north along Florida and then northeast across the Atlantic. In the cold far north it hands its heat to the air, and westerly winds carry that warmth to Europe. Now cold and salty, it sinks and joins the deep conveyor, where one lap takes about 1,000 years.
- **Tested by:**
  - L33 `question.oceans.033.q1`: About how long does a cubic meter of water take to complete the global ocean conveyor belt? → **About 1,000 years**
  - L40 `question.oceans.040.q2`: Currents and Climate recap: in what order does our warm parcel travel? → **Wind-driven current, Gulf Stream north, then sinking into the conveyor**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA's ocean conveyor explainer and educational summaries give about 1,000 years for water to complete one circuit of the slow global conveyor belt. Sources: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_currents/05conveyor2.html, https://science.nasa.gov/kids/earth/how-are-earths-ocean-and-climate-connected

### ☐ `fact.oceans.waves_size_three_factors`: unverified

> **Claim:** Wind-wave size depends on wind speed, how long the wind blows, and the fetch (the distance over water it blows in one direction); large waves form only when all three combine, so a strong wind lasting only minutes, or a long blow over a short fetch, makes no large waves.

- **Concept:** How wind builds waves (`concept.oceans.wave_wind_recipe`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L21 “How Waves Form” · `card.oceans.021.c2` (text): Wind's three ingredients / Most ocean waves start with wind rubbing on the water's surface. How big they grow takes three things: how fast the wind blows, how long it keeps blowing, and its fetch, the distance it travels over water in one direction. Large waves need all three at once. A fierce gust for a few minutes won't do it, and neither will a long gale over a short stretch of water. Your bathtub, sadly, has no fetch. / Big waves = strong wind + long time + long fetch
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Waves and Tides” · `card.oceans.030.c3` (comparison): Three ways the sea rises: Wind waves (Wind speed, time and fetch set their size; Swell: crests more than 10 to 12 seconds apart; Break where the water is about 1.3 times their height deep) vs Tides (Moon and Sun; the Sun's pull a little under half; A crest a little over every 12 hours; Up to 16 m in the Bay of Fundy) vs Storm surge (A storm's winds push water ashore; Surge plus tide makes the storm tide)
- **Tested by:**
  - L21 `question.oceans.021.q1`: Which three things decide how big wind-driven waves can grow? → **Wind speed, how long it blows, and the fetch**
  - L30 `question.oceans.030.q3`: Waves and tides recap, from Level 21: a fierce gust blows over open sea for just a few minutes. Why are there no big waves? → **It needs speed, time and fetch together**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA's Mariners Weather Log: 'Wave height is dependent on a) wind speed; b) fetch length; and c) duration'. The NOAA tutorial: 'Large waves occur only when all three factors combine.' University of Hawaii Exploring Our Fluid Earth (sea states) gives the same three factors. Sources: https://www.vos.noaa.gov/MWL/apr_06/waves.shtml, https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_currents/03coastal1.html, https://manoa.hawaii.edu/exploringourfluidearth/physical/waves/sea-states

### ☐ `fact.oceans.air_spaces_crushed`: unverified

> **Claim:** Water is nearly incompressible, but air is not: enough pressure would collapse air-filled spaces such as human lungs and the air spaces in our heads.

- **Concept:** Pressure crushes air spaces (`concept.oceans.pressure_squeezes_air`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L9 “Pressure” · `card.oceans.009.c4` (text): Why the cup shrinks / Water itself barely squeezes, but air does. Foam is full of tiny air pockets, and deep-sea pressure crushes them, so the cup shrinks and never bounces back. Your lungs and the air spaces in your head are air pockets too, and enough pressure would collapse them. That shrunken cup is a warning in miniature.
  - L60 “Checkpoint: The Deep” · `card.oceans.060.c2` (text): Pressure: be mostly water / Level 9's foam cup shrank because air squeezes. Most deep-sea animals are largely water, which barely compresses, and many have no air-filled spaces, like lungs or swim bladders, to crush. Some animals even migrate 1,000 m up and down every day, through a 100-atmosphere swing, with no harm done. Their secret is having nothing to squash.
  - L85 “Diving Helmets” · `card.oceans.085.c2` (text): Fresh air, delivered / Edmond Halley, who ran a diving company salvaging shipwrecks, fixed that by sending fresh air down in barrels, while used air escaped through a stopcock in the top. In the late 18th century, engineer John Smeaton fitted an air pump to a bell. And remember Level 9: water barely squeezes, but air does, and pressure climbs one atmosphere every 10 m. The deeper the bell, the harder the sea leaned on its air.
- **Tested by:**
  - L9 `question.oceans.009.q2`: Deep-sea pressure shrinks a foam cup, but the water around it hardly shrinks at all. Why? → **Air in the foam compresses; water barely does**
  - L60 `question.oceans.060.q2`: Deep recap: pressure crushes a foam cup's air pockets. Why doesn't it crush most deep-sea animals? → **They are mostly water, with no air spaces to crush**
  - L85 `question.oceans.085.q3`: From Level 9: as a diving bell is lowered deeper, what happens to the air trapped inside it? → **Water pressure squeezes it harder**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA Ocean Exploration: water is incompressible, and organisms with gas-filled spaces like humans would be crushed at deep-sea pressures. Sources: https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/animal-pressure/, https://www.whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-facts/why-is-pressure-different-in-the-ocean/

## How does pressure change with ocean depth? (NOAA National Ocean Service)

- **Source:** `source.noaa_pressure_depth`
- **URL:** https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/pressure.html
- **License:** US_gov_public_domain · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.oceans.pressure_1atm_per_10m`: unverified

> **Claim:** Pressure in the ocean increases by about one atmosphere, the pressure of the air at sea level, for every 10 m of depth.

- **Concept:** Pressure grows with depth (`concept.oceans.water_pressure_depth`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L9 “Pressure” · `card.oceans.009.c2` (text): A weight that stacks up / The answer is pressure. At the surface, the air above you already presses on you with one atmosphere. Every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere more. So at just 10 m down, the pressure on a diver is double what it is at the surface. You don't have to go deep to feel the ocean leaning on you.
  - L9 “Pressure” · `card.oceans.009.c3` (text): Counting atmospheres / Keep going and the atmospheres pile up in a steady stack. Water adds about 10 atmospheres at 100 m, and about 200 at 2,000 m. The rule is simple arithmetic: divide the depth in meters by 10, and you have the pressure the water adds, in atmospheres. Easy to count. Much harder to survive.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: The Blue Planet” · `card.oceans.010.c3` (text): Take the plunge / Now dive into the real thing. At the top, warm water floats over the thermocline, where the temperature drops fast. A few meters down, the red light is gone. By about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis, and past 1,000 m there's no sunlight at all. All the way, pressure climbs about one atmosphere every 10 m, until you reach the average sea floor about 3,700 m down.
  - L14 “Trenches” · `card.oceans.014.c4` (text): The deepest squeeze / Remember Level 9's rule: about one extra atmosphere of pressure for every 10 m of seawater. Now run it at Challenger Deep, about 10,935 m below the surface. The water there adds more than 1,000 atmospheres. It's the deepest spot in the ocean, so it's also the heaviest stack of water on the planet.
  - L16 “Hydrothermal Vents” · `card.oceans.016.c3` (fact): Vent water can reach about 400°C and still not boil. / That's four times the 100°C at which water boils at sea level. The trick is pressure. Remember Level 9: every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere, and the ridge crests where most vents sit lie about 2.6 km down. Squeezed that hard, the water stays liquid. Your kettle would be jealous.
  - L19 “Tsunamis” · `card.oceans.019.c4` (text): Listening on the sea floor / So how do you catch one mid-ocean? NOAA's DART stations put a pressure recorder on the sea floor. Remember Level 9: pressure comes from the water above you, about one atmosphere per 10 m. A tsunami moves the whole water column, so as it passes, the water overhead changes, and the recorder feels it. It can detect a tsunami as small as 1 cm in 6,000 m of water.
  - L85 “Diving Helmets” · `card.oceans.085.c2` (text): Fresh air, delivered / Edmond Halley, who ran a diving company salvaging shipwrecks, fixed that by sending fresh air down in barrels, while used air escaped through a stopcock in the top. In the late 18th century, engineer John Smeaton fitted an air pump to a bell. And remember Level 9: water barely squeezes, but air does, and pressure climbs one atmosphere every 10 m. The deeper the bell, the harder the sea leaned on its air.
  - L88 “The Deepest Dive” · `card.oceans.088.c3` (text): Twenty minutes at the bottom / The trip down took nearly five hours. Trieste reported about 10,916 m, the crew stayed about 20 minutes, then dropped ballast for a rise of more than three hours. HMS Challenger's rope had found 8,184 m there in 1875. Use Level 9's rule and divide by 10: the water was pressing with roughly 1,090 atmospheres.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Exploring the Ocean” · `card.oceans.090.c4` (text): Two problems: distance and depth / Every explorer here fought distance or depth. Distance gave way to stars and then clocks: latitude from a star's height, longitude from home time at 15° per hour. Depth was harder, because pressure climbs one atmosphere every 10 m. Scuba answers it by matching the water's pressure with a demand regulator. Trieste shut it out, keeping its crew inside a heavy steel cabin built to resist the deep.

Ordinary waves plus bad timing: one extraordinary wave.

### ☐ `fact.oceans.beach_sand_tan_color`: unverified

### ☐ `fact.oceans.surge_definition_wind`: unverified

> **Claim:** Storm surge is the rise in sea level caused solely by a storm, mainly by the storm's winds pushing water onshore.

- **Concept:** What makes a storm surge (`concept.oceans.storm_surge_cause`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L29 “Storm Surges” · `card.oceans.029.c1` (text): In 2005, the sea rose 27.8 feet at Pass Christian, Mississippi. / That's about 8.5 m of seawater, the highest mark of Hurricane Katrina's storm surge. The wind did most of the lifting. How?
  - L29 “Storm Surges” · `card.oceans.029.c2` (text): Wind piles up the sea / A storm surge is the rise in sea level caused by the storm itself, mainly by its winds shoving water toward the shore. Out in deep water, the pushed water can circulate down and away. Near the coast, the sea floor blocks it, so the water has nowhere to go but up and inland. A gently sloping shelf or a curved-in bay makes the surge bigger. Think of blowing across a bowl of soup: the soup climbs the far side.

- **Tested by:**
  - L29 `question.oceans.029.q2`: Why does a storm surge pile up so high on a shallow coast? → **The sea floor blocks it, so it rises and moves inland**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA's National Hurricane Center defines storm surge as an abnormal rise of water generated by a storm, over and above the predicted astronomical tide. Sources: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/surge/

### ☐ `fact.oceans.thermocline_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** A thermocline is the transition layer between warmer mixed water at the ocean's surface and much colder deep water, where temperature drops rapidly with depth.

- **Concept:** The thermocline (`concept.oceans.thermocline`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L6 “Layers of Water” · `card.oceans.006.c4` (text): The thermocline: a cold step down / Between the warm, well-mixed surface water and the much colder deep water sits the thermocline, a layer where the temperature drops fast as you go down. It isn't the same everywhere. It's semi-permanent in the tropics, shifts with the seasons in temperate seas, and is shallow or missing altogether in polar seas.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: The Blue Planet” · `card.oceans.010.c3` (text): Take the plunge / Now dive into the real thing. At the top, warm water floats over the thermocline, where the temperature drops fast. A few meters down, the red light is gone. By about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis, and past 1,000 m there's no sunlight at all. All the way, pressure climbs about one atmosphere every 10 m, until you reach the average sea floor about 3,700 m down.
  - L35 “Warm Seas, Big Storms” · `card.oceans.035.c4` (text): The storm cools the sea behind it / Remember Level 6: warm water sits on top of a much colder layer, with the thermocline between. A hurricane's winds churn up that cooler water from below, so the sea it leaves behind can be several degrees Celsius cooler. The storm literally burns through its own fuel as it goes, leaving a cold wake.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica defines the thermocline as the oceanic water layer in which temperature decreases rapidly with increasing depth, beneath a warm, well-mixed surface layer. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.tides_lunar_day_2450`: unverified

> **Claim:** A lunar day, the time for a spot on Earth to come back under the Moon, is 24 hours and 50 minutes: the Moon orbits in the direction Earth spins, so Earth needs an extra 50 minutes to catch up, and the tides run about 50 minutes later each day.

- **Concept:** Tides run on lunar days (`concept.oceans.tides_lunar_day`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L24 “Tides” · `card.oceans.024.c1` (text): High tide is late. Every single day. / Check a tide table for a week. Each day, high tide shows up about 50 minutes later than the day before. The sea isn't slacking. It's keeping an appointment with the Moon.
  - L24 “Tides” · `card.oceans.024.c3` (text): Chasing the Moon / Why the daily delay? While Earth spins, the Moon moves along its orbit in the same direction. So after one full turn, your beach has to turn a little farther to get back under the Moon. That catch-up takes 50 minutes, which makes a lunar day 24 hours and 50 minutes long. The tides keep lunar time, so on our clocks they slide about 50 minutes later every day.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NASA's tides page gives a high-to-high cycle of a little over 12 hours (two per lunar day); Astronomy Level 17 uses 24 hours and 50 minutes. Tide tables show high tides roughly 50 minutes later each day. Sources: https://science.nasa.gov/moon/tides/, https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_tides/tides05_lunarday.html

> **Claim:** Unlike wind waves, which stir only the top layer of the ocean, a tsunami moves the entire water column, from the surface to the sea floor.

Trenches like Level 14's can set them off: subduction-zone earthquakes caused the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan. A wind wave wrinkles the ocean's skin. A tsunami moves the whole body.

Remember Level 9: pressure comes from the water above you, about one atmosphere per 10 m. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.vent_400c_no_boil`: unverified

> **Claim:** Vent fluid can reach about 400°C, four times the 100°C at which water boils at sea level, yet it does not boil, because of the extreme pressure at the depths where vents form.

Your kettle would be jealous.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: The Ocean Floor” · `card.oceans.020.c3` (text): Minus 2,000 to 3,000 m: the ridge / Keep draining, and at 2,000 to 3,000 m the mid-ocean ridges start to appear: a seam about 65,000 km long, stitched around the planet. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.salt_from_weathered_rock`: unverified

> **Claim:** Rain holds dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic, so it breaks down rocks on land; streams and rivers carry the released salts to the ocean.

- **Concept:** Where sea salt comes from (`concept.oceans.salt_sources`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L5 “Why the Sea Is Salty” · `card.oceans.005.c1` (text): Dry out the ocean and the leftover salt would bury every continent. / Spread the ocean's salt evenly over all the land and it would form a layer about as tall as a 40-story office building. That's a lot of seasoning. Where did it all come from? Mostly from rocks on land.
  - L5 “Why the Sea Is Salty” · `card.oceans.005.c3` (text): Rivers deliver, the sea keeps / Rain holds a little dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic, so over time it breaks down rocks on land. Streams and rivers carry the freed salts to the sea. River water has salt in it too, just far too little to taste. At sea, water evaporates but the salt is left behind, so delivery after delivery, it builds up. The river passes the salt along; the ocean hangs on to it.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: The Blue Planet” · `card.oceans.010.c4` (text): Salty all the way down / Every liter of that dive is salty: about 35 parts per thousand, mostly chloride and sodium, washed off the land by rivers and pushed up through sea-floor vents. Weathering and erosion break rocks down over thousands or even millions of years, and streams and rivers carry the pieces toward the sea, grinding them smaller on the way. Remember Level 5, where rivers carried salt from broken-down rock to the sea? The same rivers deliver sand. Quartz is hard, doesn't split easily and barely dissolves, so it outlasts other minerals and is by far the commonest mineral in sand. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.challenger_1875_sounding`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1875, in the Mariana Trench, Challenger's rope sounding reached 4,475 fathoms (8,184 m), the deepest point known at the time.

- **Concept:** The HMS Challenger expedition (`concept.oceans.challenger_expedition`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L84 “The Challenger Expedition” · `card.oceans.084.c3` (text): Measuring the deep with rope / How do you measure water you can't see the bottom of? Challenger's crew lowered a weighted rope until it hit the sea floor, and the ship carried dredging ropes more than 7 km long. In 1875, in the Mariana Trench, one sounding reached 4,475 fathoms (8,184 m), the deepest then known. That trench's deepest spot is now called Challenger Deep, named for a later survey ship, Challenger II, in 1951. Level 2 put it at about 11 km.
  - L88 “The Deepest Dive” · `card.oceans.088.c3` (text): Twenty minutes at the bottom / The trip down took nearly five hours. Trieste reported about 10,916 m, the crew stayed about 20 minutes, then dropped ballast for a rise of more than three hours. HMS Challenger's rope had found 8,184 m there in 1875. Use Level 9's rule and divide by 10: the water was pressing with roughly 1,090 atmospheres.

### ☐ `fact.oceans.vent_how_form`: unverified

> **Claim:** At a hydrothermal vent, seawater seeps down through cracks in the ocean crust, is heated by magma below, and rises back out as a hot spring; most vents are along mid-ocean ridges.

- **Concept:** Hydrothermal vents: hot springs of the sea floor (`concept.oceans.seafloor_hot_springs`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L16 “Hydrothermal Vents” · `card.oceans.016.c2` (text): Plumbing made of rock / A hydrothermal vent is a loop. Seawater seeps down through cracks in the ocean crust, gets heated by magma below, and rises back out as a hot spring. Most vents sit along the mid-ocean ridges, which makes sense after Level 13: that's where plates push apart and magma rises. The ocean pours in cold and comes back out hot.
  - L16 “Hydrothermal Vents” · `card.oceans.016.c3` (fact): Vent water can reach about 400°C and still not boil. / That's four times the 100°C at which water boils at sea level. The trick is pressure. Remember Level 9: every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere, and the ridge crests where most vents sit lie about 2.6 km down. Squeezed that hard, the water stays liquid. Your kettle would be jealous.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: The Ocean Floor” · `card.oceans.020.c3` (text): Minus 2,000 to 3,000 m: the ridge / Keep draining, and at 2,000 to 3,000 m the mid-ocean ridges start to appear: a seam about 65,000 km long, stitched around the planet. Along it, seawater sinks into cracks, is heated by magma and gushes back out of hydrothermal vents at up to about 400°C, kept liquid only by the pressure of the ocean above.
- **Tested by:**
  - L16 `question.oceans.016.q1`: Where does the heat in a hydrothermal vent's water come from? → **Magma beneath the sea floor**
  - L16 `question.oceans.016.q2`: Vent water can reach about 400°C. Why doesn't it boil away? → **The deep ocean's pressure keeps it liquid**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. WHOI: cold seawater sinks into the seafloor through cracks, is heated by magma and flows back up; Britannica: vents are common near mid-ocean ridges. Sources: https://www.whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-topics/how-the-ocean-works/seafloor-below/hydrothermal-vents/, https://www.britannica.com/science/oceanic-ridge

> **Claim:** Sailing north toward Hawaiʻi, the Southern Cross sits lower each night; at Hawaiʻi's latitude the gap between its top and bottom stars equals the gap from the bottom star to the horizon.

European sailors used the height of the Sun or the pole star, measuring its angle above the horizon with an instrument such as a sextant. Wayfinders read the same clue. ## What is longitude? (Royal Museums Greenwich)

- **Source:** `source.rmg_what_is_longitude`
- **URL:** https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/topics/what-longitude
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.oceans.navigation_latitude_star_height`: unverified

> **Claim:** Latitude can be found from the height of the Sun or the pole star; a sextant measures a star's angle above the horizon, which estimates the observer's latitude.

- **Concept:** Latitude from stars, longitude from clocks (`concept.oceans.navigation_latitude_longitude`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L82 “Steering by the Stars” · `card.oceans.082.c3` (text): How high tells you how far / Stars also give you latitude: how far north or south you are. European sailors used the height of the Sun or the pole star, measuring its angle above the horizon with an instrument such as a sextant. Wayfinders read the same clue. Sailing north toward Hawaiʻi, the Southern Cross sits lower each night, and at Hawaiʻi's latitude the gap between its top and bottom stars matches the gap from the bottom star to the horizon.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Exploring the Ocean” · `card.oceans.090.c4` (text): Two problems: distance and depth / Every explorer here fought distance or depth. Distance gave way to stars and then clocks: latitude from a star's height, longitude from home time at 15° per hour. Depth was harder, because pressure climbs one atmosphere every 10 m. Scuba answers it by matching the water's pressure with a demand regulator. Trieste shut it out, keeping its crew inside a heavy steel cabin built to resist the deep.
- **Tested by:**
  - L82 `question.oceans.082.q3`: From Level 81, canoes sailed the long sea road from Tahiti to Hawaiʻi. Heading north, how can a wayfinder tell she has reached Hawaiʻi's latitude? → **The Southern Cross's two gaps become equal**
  - L90 `question.oceans.090.q4`: Exploring the Ocean recap, from Level 82: what did a clock keeping home time let sailors work out? → **Their longitude**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. A Yale Teachers Institute unit and an arXiv paper on Polaris note the rule that Polaris's elevation, measured by sextant, quadrant or astrolabe, approximately equals latitude. > **Claim:** Longitude has no natural starting line, but Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so each hour of difference between local time and home time equals 15° of longitude.

You just needed a clock that kept home time at sea, and pendulum clocks were useless on a rolling ship. Britain's 1714 Longitude Act offered rewards. John Harrison, a self-taught clockmaker, built H4, trialled on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761. Where am I? First ask: what time is it at home?
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Exploring the Ocean” · `card.oceans.090.c4` (text): Two problems: distance and depth / Every explorer here fought distance or depth. Distance gave way to stars and then clocks: latitude from a star's height, longitude from home time at 15° per hour. Depth was harder, because pressure climbs one atmosphere every 10 m. ## 10.3 Waves on the Shore (Introduction to Oceanography, Paul Webb) (Roger Williams University Open Publishing)

- **Source:** `source.rwu_webb_waves_shore`

### ☐ `fact.oceans.waves_crest_outruns_base`: unverified

> **Claim:** Near shore, friction with the bottom slows the lower part of a wave while the crest keeps its speed, so the wave steepens until the crest, with no water beneath it, topples forward as a breaker.

- **Concept:** Why waves break (`concept.oceans.wave_breaking`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L22 “Why Waves Break” · `card.oceans.022.c3` (text): The top outruns the bottom / Friction holds back the bottom of the wave, but the crest keeps its speed. The front grows steeper and steeper until the crest is racing ahead with no water underneath it, and it topples forward. That's a breaker. As a rule of thumb, it happens where the water is about 1.3 times as deep as the wave is tall: a 1 m wave breaks in water about 1.3 m deep.
- **Tested by:**
  - L22 `question.oceans.022.q2`: Near the beach, why does the crest of a wave topple forward? → **The bottom slows, but the crest keeps going**
  - L22 `question.oceans.022.q3`: From Level 21: swell can cross an ocean with little energy lost. Where does that long trip finally end? → **In shallow water, where the slowed wave breaks**
  - L30 `question.oceans.030.q4`: Waves and tides recap, from Level 22: a 2 m wave heads for shore. About how deep is the water where it breaks? → **About 2.6 m**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA defines breakers as waves that become too steep and unstable; oceanography texts describe the crest getting ahead of the slowed base with no water underneath. Sources: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_currents/03coastal1.html, https://rwu.pressbooks.pub/webboceanography/chapter/10-3-waves-on-the-shore/

### ☐ `fact.oceans.waves_shoaling_shorter_taller`: unverified

> **Claim:** As a wave touches bottom it slows; the waves behind catch up, so the wavelength shortens, and with the same energy the wave grows taller.

- **Concept:** Waves feel the bottom (`concept.oceans.wave_shoaling`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L22 “Why Waves Break” · `card.oceans.022.c2` (text): The wave feels the floor / Remember Level 21's circles of moving water, fading out about half a wavelength down? Once the sea gets shallower than that, the circles scrape the bottom and flatten. The wave slows. The waves behind catch up, so they bunch closer together, and the same energy squeezed into less room makes each wave taller. Near the beach, waves hit a traffic jam and pile up.
- **Tested by:**
  - L22 `question.oceans.022.q1`: A wave starts to feel the sea floor when the water gets shallower than what? → **About half its wavelength**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. LibreTexts (Stewart, Introduction to Physical Oceanography) and standard references on wave shoaling: in shallower water speed and wavelength decrease while wave height increases. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.navigation_latitude_star_height`: unverified

> **Claim:** Latitude can be found from the height of the Sun or the pole star; a sextant measures a star's angle above the horizon, which estimates the observer's latitude.

- **Concept:** Latitude from stars, longitude from clocks (`concept.oceans.navigation_latitude_longitude`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L82 “Steering by the Stars” · `card.oceans.082.c3` (text): How high tells you how far / Stars also give you latitude: how far north or south you are. European sailors used the height of the Sun or the pole star, measuring its angle above the horizon with an instrument such as a sextant. Wayfinders read the same clue. Sailing north toward Hawaiʻi, the Southern Cross sits lower each night, and at Hawaiʻi's latitude the gap between its top and bottom stars matches the gap from the bottom star to the horizon.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Exploring the Ocean” · `card.oceans.090.c4` (text): Two problems: distance and depth / Every explorer here fought distance or depth. Distance gave way to stars and then clocks: latitude from a star's height, longitude from home time at 15° per hour. Depth was harder, because pressure climbs one atmosphere every 10 m. Scuba answers it by matching the water's pressure with a demand regulator. Trieste shut it out, keeping its crew inside a heavy steel cabin built to resist the deep.
- **Tested by:**
  - L82 `question.oceans.082.q3`: From Level 81, canoes sailed the long sea road from Tahiti to Hawaiʻi. Heading north, how can a wayfinder tell she has reached Hawaiʻi's latitude? → **The Southern Cross's two gaps become equal**
  - L90 `question.oceans.090.q4`: Exploring the Ocean recap, from Level 82: what did a clock keeping home time let sailors work out? → **Their longitude**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. A Yale Teachers Institute unit and an arXiv paper on Polaris note the rule that Polaris's elevation, measured by sextant, quadrant or astrolabe, approximately equals latitude. Sources: https://teachersinstitute.yale.edu/curriculum/units/files/07.03.09.pdf, https://arxiv.org/html/2206.07491v1

### ☐ `fact.oceans.magnetic_stripes_symmetric`: unverified

> **Claim:** The ocean floor shows stripes of rock with alternating magnetic direction, running parallel to the mid-ocean ridge and matching on either side of it, because Earth's magnetic field has flipped many times.

- **Concept:** Magnetic stripes on the sea floor (`concept.oceans.seafloor_magnetic_stripes`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c3` (text): Stripes on the sea floor / The evidence was written in magnetism. As lava cools into rock, grains of a magnetic mineral called magnetite lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field, and that field has flipped many times. So the ocean floor carries stripes of alternating magnetic direction, running parallel to the ridge and matching on both sides of it. New rock forms in the middle and moves off both ways, like a barcode printed twice in mirror image.
- **Tested by:**
  - L18 `question.oceans.018.q2`: Why do the magnetic stripes on one side of a mid-ocean ridge mirror those on the other? → **New rock forms at the crest and moves off both ways, recording the field**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica: magnetic anomalies alternate with distance from the ridge axis and are nearly symmetrically arranged on both sides of it. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/seafloor-spreading
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.oceans.spreading_hess_1960`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1960, geophysicist Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading: new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and old ocean floor sinks back into the trenches, so the ocean basins are constantly recycled and Earth doesn't get bigger.

- **Concept:** The sea floor's conveyor belt (`concept.oceans.seafloor_spreading_cycle`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c2` (text): A conveyor belt of rock / In 1960, geophysicist Harry Hess proposed an answer: seafloor spreading. New ocean floor forms at the mid-ocean ridges, where Level 13's magma rises. Old ocean floor sinks back down into the trenches of Level 14. The ocean basins are constantly recycled, which is also why Earth doesn't keep getting bigger. Ridges are where the conveyor belt comes out; trenches are where it goes back in.
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c3` (text): Stripes on the sea floor / The evidence was written in magnetism. As lava cools into rock, grains of a magnetic mineral called magnetite lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field, and that field has flipped many times. So the ocean floor carries stripes of alternating magnetic direction, running parallel to the ridge and matching on both sides of it. New rock forms in the middle and moves off both ways, like a barcode printed twice in mirror image.
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c4` (text): Older, deeper, gone / Walk away from a ridge and the floor gets older: youngest at the crest, older farther out. Level 15's guyots showed it sinks as it travels, too. Very little ocean floor is older than 150 million years, and the oldest known, about 200 million years old, lies in the far western Pacific. After that, it's back down a trench.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: The Ocean Floor” · `card.oceans.020.c4` (text): Minus 6,000 m: only the trenches / By 6,000 m, most of the ocean is gone. The flat abyssal plains lie bare under their blanket of ooze, and only the trenches still hold water, down to about 11 km at Challenger Deep. That's where old sea floor sinks back down, while the ridges make new floor. Drained, the floor tells one story: made at the ridges, buried in snow, swallowed by the trenches.
- **Tested by:**
  - L18 `question.oceans.018.q1`: In seafloor spreading, what happens to old ocean floor? → **It sinks back down into the trenches**
  - L18 `question.oceans.018.q3`: From Level 15: guyots are old islands now 1,000 to 2,000 m down. What does seafloor spreading add to their story? → **The floor sinks as it moves from the ridge, carrying them down**
  - L20 `question.oceans.020.q3`: Ocean Floor recap, from Level 18: why is no ocean floor older than about 200 million years? → **Old floor sinks back into trenches as ridges make new floor**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. USGS This Dynamic Earth describes Hess's early-1960s idea that crust made at ridges is consumed in trenches, explaining why Earth does not grow; NOAA Science On a Sphere describes the same recycling. Sources: https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/developing.html, https://sos.noaa.gov/catalog/datasets/age-of-the-seafloor/

### ☐ `fact.oceans.tsunami_whole_column`: unverified

> **Claim:** Unlike wind waves, which stir only the top layer of the ocean, a tsunami moves the entire water column, from the surface to the sea floor.

- **Concept:** How tsunamis cross oceans (`concept.oceans.tsunami_ocean_crossing`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L19 “Tsunamis” · `card.oceans.019.c2` (text): The whole ocean moves / Wind waves stir only the top layer of the ocean. A tsunami is different: it moves the entire water column, from the surface all the way down to the sea floor. Trenches like Level 14's can set them off: subduction-zone earthquakes caused the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan. A wind wave wrinkles the ocean's skin. A tsunami moves the whole body.
  - L19 “Tsunamis” · `card.oceans.019.c4` (text): Listening on the sea floor / So how do you catch one mid-ocean? NOAA's DART stations put a pressure recorder on the sea floor. Remember Level 9: pressure comes from the water above you, about one atmosphere per 10 m. A tsunami moves the whole water column, so as it passes, the water overhead changes, and the recorder feels it. It can detect a tsunami as small as 1 cm in 6,000 m of water.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA's JetStream: unlike wind-driven waves, tsunamis move through the entire water column, from the ocean floor to the surface. ### ☐ `fact.oceans.salt_from_weathered_rock`: unverified

> **Claim:** Rain holds dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic, so it breaks down rocks on land; streams and rivers carry the released salts to the ocean.

That's a lot of seasoning. Where did it all come from? Mostly from rocks on land.
  - L5 “Why the Sea Is Salty” · `card.oceans.005.c3` (text): Rivers deliver, the sea keeps / Rain holds a little dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic, so over time it breaks down rocks on land. Streams and rivers carry the freed salts to the sea. River water has salt in it too, just far too little to taste. At sea, water evaporates but the salt is left behind, so delivery after delivery, it builds up. The river passes the salt along; the ocean hangs on to it.

Weathering and erosion break rocks down over thousands or even millions of years, and streams and rivers carry the pieces toward the sea, grinding them smaller on the way. > **Claim:** Oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer and NOAA's James Ingraham used the toys' landings to test a computer model that works out surface currents from the winds.

### ☐ `fact.oceans.southern_acc_barrier`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Antarctic Circumpolar Current acts as a barrier, separating the Southern Ocean from the waters to its north.

- **Concept:** The Antarctic Circumpolar Current (`concept.oceans.southern_circumpolar_current`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L74 “The Southern Ocean” · `card.oceans.074.c2` (text): An ocean fenced by a current / Remember Level 3: the Southern Ocean is the one defined by a current, with its northern edge at 60° south. That current is the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the largest wind-driven current on Earth. It flows west to east all the way around Antarctica, the only current that circles the planet, linking the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans. It also works as a barrier, keeping the Southern Ocean apart from the waters to its north.
- **Tested by:**
  - L74 `question.oceans.074.q1`: Which way does the Antarctic Circumpolar Current flow? → **West to east, all the way around Antarctica**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica says the current 'separates the Southern Ocean from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans'; The Conversation's explainer describes it as isolating Antarctica from warmer waters. - **URL:** https://www.whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-facts/how-is-beach-sand-created/
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.oceans.beach_sand_tan_color`: unverified

> **Claim:** The tan color of most sand beaches comes from quartz tinted light brown by iron oxide, plus feldspar.

- **Concept:** Beach sand from worn-down rock (`concept.oceans.beach_sand_from_rock`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L61 “Beaches” · `card.oceans.061.c2` (text): Mountains, delivered in pieces / Most sand starts as rock. Weathering and erosion break rocks down over thousands or even millions of years, and streams and rivers carry the pieces toward the sea, grinding them smaller on the way. Remember Level 5, where rivers carried salt from broken-down rock to the sea? The same rivers deliver sand. Quartz is hard, doesn't split easily and barely dissolves, so it outlasts other minerals and is by far the commonest mineral in sand. A tan beach is mostly quartz, tinted by iron oxide, plus feldspar: the toughest leftovers of old rock.
  - L61 “Beaches” · `card.oceans.061.c3` (comparison): Read a beach by its color: Tan (Quartz tinted light brown by iron oxide, plus feldspar; Worn from rock and carried down by rivers) vs Black (Lava that cools and shatters as it enters the sea; Hawaii's famous black sand) vs Pink (Crushed shells of foraminifera, single-celled sea creatures; Bermuda's pink beaches)
- **Tested by:**
  - L61 `question.oceans.061.q2`: Why is quartz by far the commonest mineral in most beach sand? → **It's hard and barely dissolves, so it outlasts the rest**
  - L61 `question.oceans.061.q3`: From Level 5: rain breaks down rock and rivers carry the salt to the sea. What else do those same rivers carry to the coast? → **Worn-down bits of rock that become sand**
  - L62 `question.oceans.062.q3`: From Level 61: sand is rock worn down to small grains. How do waves turn that sand against a sea cliff? → **They hurl it at the rock, grinding the cliff down**
  - L69 `question.oceans.069.q3`: From Level 61: rivers carry worn-down rock to the coast as sand. What happens to a coast when that supply is cut off? → **It erodes and moves inland**
  - L70 `question.oceans.070.q5`: Coasts and Islands recap, from Levels 61 and 69: what do rivers supply that keeps many beaches from wasting away? → **Sand worn from rock farther inland**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NOAA and WHOI give the same explanation independently: iron oxide tints quartz light brown and feldspar is tan. Sources: https://www.whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-facts/how-is-beach-sand-created/, https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/sand.html

### ☐ `fact.oceans.ridge_plates_apart`: unverified

> **Claim:** At a mid-ocean ridge, plates push apart and magma rises to fill the gap, building new sea floor.

- **Concept:** The mid-ocean ridge (`concept.oceans.mid_ocean_ridge`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L13 “Mid-Ocean Ridges” · `card.oceans.013.c3` (text): A mountain range that builds sea floor / The ridge is the largest single volcanic feature on Earth: thousands of volcanoes and volcanic ridge segments that erupt from time to time. It rises from sea floor about 5 km deep to crests about 2.6 km below the surface. Along it, plates push apart and magma rises to fill the gap, building brand-new sea floor. The ridge isn't just scenery. It's a factory.
  - L13 “Mid-Ocean Ridges” · `card.oceans.013.c4` (text): "Girl talk" / Tharp's colleague Bruce Heezen at first dismissed her valley as "girl talk". By 1953 he was convinced: the locations of earthquakes turned out to line up inside it. The valley was real, and it ran right along the seam where the plates push apart. Tharp had found where the sea floor is made.
  - L14 “Trenches” · `card.oceans.014.c2` (text): Where the sea floor goes back down / Trenches form where two plates converge. The older, denser plate is pushed down beneath the lighter one and plunges into the mantle, and the sea floor above the bend becomes a long, narrow, very deep trench. Most trenches are in the Pacific. If Level 13's ridges are where plates push apart to build sea floor, trenches are where sea floor heads back down into Earth.
  - L16 “Hydrothermal Vents” · `card.oceans.016.c2` (text): Plumbing made of rock / A hydrothermal vent is a loop. Seawater seeps down through cracks in the ocean crust, gets heated by magma below, and rises back out as a hot spring. Most vents sit along the mid-ocean ridges, which makes sense after Level 13: that's where plates push apart and magma rises. The ocean pours in cold and comes back out hot.
  - L18 “The Spreading Sea Floor” · `card.oceans.018.c2` (text): A conveyor belt of rock / In 1960, geophysicist Harry Hess proposed an answer: seafloor spreading. New ocean floor forms at the mid-ocean ridges, where Level 13's magma rises. Old ocean floor sinks back down into the trenches of Level 14. The ocean basins are constantly recycled, which is also why Earth doesn't keep getting bigger. Ridges are where the conveyor belt comes out; trenches are where it goes back in.

  - L20 `question.oceans.020.q2`: Ocean Floor recap: why do the mid-ocean ridges show up before the abyssal plains as NASA's ocean drains? → **Ridge crests sit about 2.6 km deep; plains lie 3,000 to 6,000 m down**

By about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis, and past 1,000 m there's no sunlight at all.
